system:
You are a senior SOC analyst investigating Kubernetes activity. Work only from evidence returned by your tools; never invent event IDs, IPs or principals.

Scope: one day (2026-10-14) of Kubernetes API audit logs for the payments-prod cluster, which runs on AWS (EKS), GCP (GKE) and Azure (AKS).

Data: ocsf_api_activity holds all three clouds normalized to the OCSF API Activity schema (one row per audit event; metadata.uid is the audit event ID). Purpose-built tools search and summarize it and look up identity, IP, service-account, cluster and allowlist context; query_sql is available for anything else.

Method: start broad, form hypotheses, verify each against the data, and check enrichment context before concluding. Cite every malicious event you rely on by its audit event ID. When finished, call submit_verdict exactly once; the investigation ends when you do.

content.text: I'll start with the alert event itself, the identity behind it, and an overview of the data.
Jordan Doe is on PTO (Oct 12–19) and usually runs darwin, but this request came from linux kubectl. Next I'll pull all human activity and everything from the source IP.

input.summary: Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com), a Payments Engineering developer on PTO 2026-10-12..19 who normally uses macOS, had stolen credentials used against payments-prod on all three clouds. Every jdoe event came from 198.51.100.23, a bulletproof VPS (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL) that threat feeds flag as malicious, using kubectl linux/amd64. The same scripted playbook ran on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34): the actor checked permissions (selfsubjectrulesreviews), listed namespaces, tried to read kube-system secrets and create a Job there (denied), then read payments/payments-db-credentials. Next it created a privileged hostPID/hostPath=/ pod 'debug-tools-7f9c' in the payments namespace and exec'd 'nsenter -t 1' into it to escape to the node. After that it used the argocd-application-controller service account token (cluster-admin, meant to run in-cluster only) from the same external IP to create a 'jdoe-break-glass' ClusterRoleBinding granting jdoe cluster-admin. With that access it planted persistence and backdoors (DaemonSet kube-system/kube-metrics-agent and CronJob kube-system/node-cert-rotate, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus NodePort service default/metrics-agent-np on port 30080), then dumped all secrets cluster-wide. Impact: all secrets in all three clusters should be treated as exposed, including payments DB credentials. Nodes were compromised and attacker workloads are still running. Both jdoe's credentials and the argocd SA token are compromised.

argocd SA creates jdoe-break-glass CRB -> cluster-admin for jdoe

benign_lookalikes: rpatel@example.com (Staff SRE, eks-sre role) created privileged hostPID node-debugger-ip-10-0-12-11-x7k2p pod (f289fe27-bc32-9165-38f0-463a6c185582) from corp VPN 203.0.113.12 with darwin kubectl: a standard 'kubectl debug node' session with an approved busybox image. It is not on the allowlist, so it is worth a policy follow-up, but it is not malicious.
Many engineers ran pods/exec into app pods (payments, ledger, checkout, etc.) from corp egress 203.0.113.x as routine operations.
Daily 03:05 clusterrolebinding updates by eks:addon-manager, system:addon-manager and aksService from control-plane IPs are managed-service reconciliation.
argocd-application-controller's in-cluster list traffic from 10.0.12.108, 10.128.0.104 and 10.224.0.102 is normal GitOps behaviour. Only its use from 198.51.100.23 is malicious.
system:anonymous probes from Palo Alto Expanse scanners (198.18/15) are internet scanning noise.

verdict.summary: Jordan Doe (jdoe@example.com), a Payments Engineering developer on PTO 2026-10-12..19 who normally uses macOS, had stolen credentials used against payments-prod on all three clouds. Every jdoe event came from 198.51.100.23, a bulletproof VPS (NIGHTOWL-HOSTING, NL) that threat feeds flag as malicious, using kubectl linux/amd64. The same scripted playbook ran on EKS (14:02-14:25), GKE (14:38-15:01) and AKS (15:11-15:34): the actor checked permissions (selfsubjectrulesreviews), listed namespaces, tried to read kube-system secrets and create a Job there (denied), then read payments/payments-db-credentials. Next it created a privileged hostPID/hostPath=/ pod 'debug-tools-7f9c' in the payments namespace and exec'd 'nsenter -t 1' into it to escape to the node. After that it used the argocd-application-controller service account token (cluster-admin, meant to run in-cluster only) from the same external IP to create a 'jdoe-break-glass' ClusterRoleBinding granting jdoe cluster-admin. With that access it planted persistence and backdoors (DaemonSet kube-system/kube-metrics-agent and CronJob kube-system/node-cert-rotate, both pulling images from 198.51.100.23:5000, plus NodePort service default/metrics-agent-np on port 30080), then dumped all secrets cluster-wide. Impact: all secrets in all three clusters should be treated as exposed, including payments DB credentials. Nodes were compromised and attacker workloads are still running. Both jdoe's credentials and the argocd SA token are compromised.
